REVIEW FINDINGS PRESERVED - NON-AUTHORIZING, NO VERDICT WAS RECORDED\n\nThis round cannot be recorded as a verdict, so none was. The reviewer findings are kept below with every parseable decision line voided. Acting on them requires a fresh governed review at this head.\n\nI have everything I need. Evidence verified; writing the review.\n---\n## Provisional verdict\n> VOIDED REVIEWER LINE - **REVISE.** The change is genuinely additive and safe with respect to the *existing* database (two new empty tables, nothing else touched, deny-by-default access). But it ships a declared \"final plm home\" that is structurally *weaker* than the landing table it replaces, and its own header rationale is contradicted by applied migrations already in this repo. Fixable without redesign.\n## Sealed-evidence verification (manifest §1–§5)\nI re-derived the packet's claims from files rather than trusting them:\n- **Patch ↔ tree agreement.** `supabase/migrations/20260925044029_plm_item_user_assignment_and_workflow_action.sql` on disk matches `patch.diff` content exactly, and the diff hunk header `@@ -0,0 +1,85 @@` matches the 85-line file. The two `.agent/work/3498/1/*.json` files match the manifest's `git diff --name-status`.\n- **Version uniqueness (§4 rule 5).** `20260925044029` is the only `20260925*` file in `supabase/migrations/` (707 files). It sorts after the base branch's newest (`20260923173715`), so Guard B and the duplicate-version check in `scripts/check-sql.sh` would both pass.\n- **Object collision.** `plm.item_user_assignment` / `plm.item_workflow_action` appear nowhere else in the repo (grep: 8 hits, all in this file). No pre-existing object to collide with.\n- **`dispatchObjectKeys` claim — verified accurate.** `completion.json` asserts the migration yields exactly the two `table plm.*` keys. I traced the extractor: `CREATE TABLE` → `table`; `COMMENT ON TABLE` → a single `table` key (`check-pr-object-collisions.mjs:626-634`, `m[1]='table'`); `ALTER TABLE … ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` → `table`. `REVOKE … ON TABLE` *does* emit both `table` and `view` keys (`:584-588`, `relationGuess`), but the same file's `CREATE TABLE` rules out the `view` half. The claim holds.\n- **`check-sql.sh` \"exit 0\" — true but near-vacuous.** Two of its three content guards cannot fire on this file: `check-expected-count-patterns.mjs` only inspects migrations using an `expected_counts` JSON object (none here), and `check-migration-verify-cost.mjs` only inspects dollar-quoted `DO` verification blocks (none here — see finding 8). The \"Static checks passed\" evidence carries almost no signal about this migration's content.\n- **Not verifiable in this profile.** `git diff --check` and the whole-source digest `4d40625a…` require a shell, which this review profile deliberately lacks (manifest §1). I confirmed content equivalence against the packet instead. Note `completion.json.head_sha` is `c5a57705…` (the implementation commit), not the PR head `87ff50ea…` (the evidence commit) — consistent with the manifest's commit table, not a discrepancy.\n- **§5: no tests were run.** Confirmed and material — see finding 10.\n## Findings\n### High — correctness and integrity\n**1. `UNIQUE (id, rfq_item_id)` (line 52) is integrity-dead *and* cannot be used as an index as written.** `id` is already the primary key (line 36), so the composite unique constraint adds no integrity guarantee whatsoever. As an access path it is equally useless: `rfq_item_id` is a non-leading column and Postgres has no skip-scan, so no predicate on `rfq_item_id` can use it, and a predicate on `id` is already served by the PK. Its *only* legitimate purpose in the dflow source is to be the target of the composite self-FK `(source_action_id, rfq_item_id) → (id, rfq_item_id)` (`20260905053422_workflow_action_handoff_integrity.sql:56-65`), which makes it structural that a return action answers a handoff on the **same** RFQ item. This migration keeps the unique key and keeps the weaker `item_workflow_action_source_action_not_self` CHECK (lines 58-59) but drops the FK the pair was built for — so it pays second-index write amplification on every insert and enforces nothing. This is the clearest instance of \"an index that exists but cannot be used as written.\"\n**2. The self-referencing FK is omitted, and the stated reason does not cover it.** The header (lines 6-8) justifies omitted FKs as \"Cross-schema foreign keys into `dflow.*` … so the plm homes do not couple to the landing schema.\" `source_action_id` would reference `plm.item_workflow_action` — the same table, the same schema, nothing to do with `dflow`. Consequence: in the declared final home, `source_action_id` may point at a nonexistent id, or at an action belonging to a *different* `rfq_item_id`, re-opening exactly defect #1 that `#2203` was written to close. This omission also cannot be explained by claim scope: `references` is not modelled by the object-key extractor at all (`check-pr-object-collisions.mjs` models `create`/`drop`/`alter index` and has no `constraint` or `references` kind), so an inline FK inside `CREATE TABLE` adds **zero** new object keys.\n**3. The FK targets for `rfq_item_id`, `prior_step_id`, `new_step_id` are already in `plm`, not `dflow` — the header's rationale is factually wrong.** Applied migration `20260904143518_canonical_designflow_workflow_contract.sql` (#2202) re-pointed them *into plm*: `dflow.item_user_assignment.rfq_item_id → plm.\"RFQItem\"(\"rfqItem_id\")` (`:10-15`), and `dflow.item_workflow_action.rfq_item_id → plm.\"RFQItem\"`, `prior_step_id`/`new_step_id → plm.\"RFQStep\"(\"RFQStep_id\")` (`:16-29`). Both targets are real tables (`supabase/ci-bootstrap/010_pre_adoption_baseline.sql:791` and `:919`). So for these three columns the canonical reference is **intra-schema** and was available at zero claim cost; the \"do not couple to the landing schema\" argument actually argues *for* pointing at `plm.\"RFQItem\"`. As written, the plm home accepts any integer as an item or step id. Genuinely cross-schema and defensibly deferred: `user_id`, `assigned_by_user_id`, `actor_user_id`, `fallback_recipient_user_id → dflow.users(id)` — no plm users table exists.\n**4. Neither table has a single usable index.** `plm.item_user_assignment` has only its PK; `plm.item_workflow_action` has only its PK, the `correlation_key` unique (line 53 — the one predicate genuinely served), and the dead unique from finding 1. Every access path the dflow originals depend on is absent:\n| Missing index | Source |\n|---|---|\n| `item_workflow_action_item_time (rfq_item_id, occurred_at, id)` | `20260901221310:40-41` |\n| `item_workflow_action_open_handoff_lookup (rfq_item_id, occurred_at desc, id desc) include (actor_user_id)` | `20260905053422:101-103` |\n| `item_workflow_action_admin_review (rfq_item_id, occurred_at) where requires_admin_review` | `20260905053422:105-107` |\n| `item_user_assignment_active_lookup (rfq_item_id, function_key, effective_from, id) include (user_id) where effective_to is null` | `20260901221310:20-23` |\n`rfq_item_id` is the leading predicate of every query against both tables (all four call sites in `dflow.record_item_workflow_action`); in `plm` it is a sequential scan. The comparison is sharpest against the sibling this migration names in its own comment (line 33, \"Beside `productUserAssignment`\"): `plm.\"productUserAssignment\"` carries `productUserAssignment_item_role_key` UNIQUE `(item_id_fk, role)` and `productUserAssignment_user_idx` (`ci-bootstrap:6285-6286`), and the adjacent plm precedent `plm.product_type_factory_time` ships `product_type_factory_time_factory_time_id_idx` (`20260911214438_plm_factory_time_templates.sql:87-88`). This is the only plm table creation in that lineage with no index at all.\n**5. Both uniqueness invariants are dropped, so the \"final home\" is weaker than the landing table.**\n- `item_user_assignment_one_active` UNIQUE `(rfq_item_id, function_key, user_id) WHERE effective_to IS NULL` (`20260901221310:17-19`) → `plm` permits **multiple simultaneously-active** assignments for the same item/function/user.\n- `item_workflow_action_one_return_per_source` UNIQUE `(source_action_id) WHERE source_action_id IS NOT NULL` (`20260905053422:96-98`) → `plm` permits one handoff to be \"returned\" an unlimited number of times. That partial unique index *is* the fix for #2203 defect #1 (\"enforced by a partial unique index rather than by convention, so one handoff can never be returned twice\").\nThe header (lines 9-10) defends this with \"this claim writes exactly the two tables.\" That misstates the repo's own policy: `dispatchObjectKeys` resolves `CREATE INDEX` to **both** `index plm.<name>` **and** `table plm.<table>` — `check-dispatch-collision.test.mjs:369-373`, with the comment \"an index is a write to its table, and the index name is itself claimable.\" Indexes are therefore separately claimable objects that should have been listed in the claim up front, per §4 (\"If you cannot list the objects up front, your task is read-only\"). The claim was authored by the same dispatch (`.agent/work/3498/1/contract.json`), so this is a self-inflicted scope cut, not an external constraint.\n### Medium\n**6. \"Column shapes match the dflow sources\" (line 6; repeated in both COMMENTs, lines 33 and 78) is untrue for two columns.** In dflow, `actor_identity_source`'s DEFAULT is an *expression* that derives provenance from the session — `case when nullif(current_setting('request.designflow.actor_id', true),'') is not null then 'designflow_jwt' else 'supabase_auth' end` — and `actor_identity_email`'s DEFAULT is `lower(btrim(coalesce(nullif(current_setting('request.designflow.actor_email', true),''), auth.jwt()->>'email')))` (`20260907121732_designflow_trusted_backend_actor.sql:12-27`). The plm version substitutes a bare literal `DEFAULT 'supabase_auth'` (line 40) and no default at all (line 41). Consequence: provenance in the plm home is no longer derived from anything, so nothing structurally prevents a DesignFlow-backend write being stamped `supabase_auth`. Combined with the retained `item_workflow_action_actor_provenance` CHECK (lines 68-74), a backend-JWT insert that omits `actor_identity_source` and has a null `actor_auth_user_id` fails the check outright, while one that happens to carry a UUID is silently mislabeled. The *types* match; the defaults and the derived-provenance guarantee do not.\n**7. Column order diverges from the source — in the table whose stated purpose is to be the copy target.** dflow's live order appends `actor_identity_source`, `actor_identity_email` **last** (added by #2496, after `requires_admin_review`); plm inserts them 5th and 6th, between `actor_auth_user_id` (line 39) and `prior_step_id` (line 42). Any positional `INSERT INTO plm.item_workflow_action SELECT * FROM dflow.item_workflow_action` in the deferred row-movement session mis-maps from column 5 onward. It fails loudly rather than silently (integer → text has no assignment cast), but it is a trap planted directly in the path this migration exists to prepare, and it further contradicts finding 6.\n**8. No exact-object assertion anywhere in the file (mandatory check #3 unmet).** The migration never asserts that the `plm` schema exists, that `plm.\"RFQItem\"`/`plm.\"RFQStep\"` exist, or that `dflow.item_user_assignment`/`dflow.item_workflow_action` exist with the columns it claims to mirror — despite line 3 asserting derivation from \"(live shapes)\". AGENTS.md §4 rule 5 is explicit: *\"Before trusting any migration, confirm the OBJECT exists (`to_regclass`) — never just the ledger row.\"* The adjacent plm precedent does exactly this with a `DO $$ … IF EXISTS … RAISE EXCEPTION … END $$` guard (`20260911214438:25-31`). No guard forbids it here: `check-migration-verify-cost.mjs` refuses only verification blocks that *read data* (`from`/`join`/`into`/`update`/`delete from`/`truncate`/`copy`/maintenance contexts, or a `search_path` reaching `plm`), and its own header states \"Shape checks belong in the catalogue\" — `to_regclass`/`pg_catalog` assertions are the expressly permitted form. In fact `plm` does exist (`20260621150714_foundation.sql:10`), so the migration applies; the gap is that nothing in the file would have caught it otherwise, and nothing verifies the resulting shape.\n**9. Append-only is asserted in a comment and enforced by nothing.** Line 78: \"Append-only workflow action history\"; line 33: \"Item function-role assignment history.\" dflow enforces both with `BEFORE UPDATE OR DELETE` triggers — `item_workflow_action_immutable` (`20260901221310:127-129`) and `item_user_assignment_immutable_history` (same file, `dflow.reject_item_assignment_history_rewrite`). The plm homes have no trigger, so the documented property is unprotected. A trigger *function* would add a `function plm.*` object key, so unlike the indexes this deferral is at least arguable — but then the comment must not assert the property, or must say it is not yet enforced.\n**10. No contract test, though the harness is free and the predecessors each have one.** `supabase/tests/designflow_item_assignment_action_history_contracts.sql`, `designflow_workflow_action_handoff_integrity_contracts.sql`, and `designflow_trusted_backend_actor_contracts.sql` cover the dflow originals. CI globs rather than lists — \"A new `supabase/tests/*.sql` file is wired into CI the moment it is committed\" (`.github/workflows/database-contract-tests.yml:30-32`) — and runs every test against an ephemeral DB with all migrations applied (`:628`, `:714`). This PR ships 8 CHECK constraints, 2 UNIQUE constraints and 2 divergent defaults with zero executable evidence, and manifest §5 confirms no tests were run.\n### Low / nits\n**11. The change leaves authoritative documentation false.** `docs/designflow-master-data-migration/designflow-schema-segregation.md:152-153` (rows 24a/24b) still say \"`plm` table not yet created\" for both tables; this migration creates them. The document-history row at `:328` records the 2026-09-24 *placement* but not the creation. AGENTS.md's session wrap-up convention requires leaving docs current. Note also `:319` (\"Recreate cross-schema FKs and verify grants/RLS\") is the documented procedure for this migration step — findings 2 and 3 are where this PR departs from it.\n**12. Volatility (mandatory check #2): no violation, one consequence worth recording.** The migration creates no functions, so there is no volatility marker that could be wrong. The only volatility-bearing construct is `clock_timestamp()` (VOLATILE) as a column DEFAULT on `effective_from` (line 20), `created_at` (line 23) and `occurred_at` (line 47) — legal in a DEFAULT, evaluated per-row at insert, and an exact match for the dflow sources. Two things to know: `effective_from` and `created_at` on the same row receive *different* timestamps (two independent evaluations), so never assume they are equal; and the adjacent plm precedent uses STABLE `now()` instead (`20260911214438:76`). Keeping `clock_timestamp()` is the right call for shape fidelity. The CHECK-constraint helpers (`lower`, `btrim`, `jsonb_typeof`, `~`) are all IMMUTABLE, which is what a CHECK requires.\n**13. No `lock_timeout` / `statement_timeout`.** Both dflow structural migrations in this lineage set them (`20260905053422:41-42`, `20260907121732:8-9`); the plm precedent `20260911214438` does not. Risk is near zero here — `CREATE TABLE` locks only brand-new objects — so this is consistency-only.\n**14. RLS and grants: compliant, but the rationale is undocumented.** Lines 80-83 (`ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` with zero policies + `REVOKE ALL … FROM PUBLIC, anon, authenticated, service_role`) exactly match the established plm access model — `20260911214438:96-99`, \"the DesignFlow API connects as the table owner. No browser or service-role access.\" They also pre-empt the zero-policy-with-grants defect remediated by `20260914155226_revoke_api_role_grants_zero_policy_tables.sql` (#2662 Part A), and are consistent with `docs/verification/database-efficiency/20260910T002917Z/api-access-matrix.md:25`, which records the dflow originals as unexposed. The precedent carries an explanatory comment; this migration does not, so a future reader cannot tell whether deny-all is deliberate or an unfinished access model. One fragility worth knowing: the `REVOKE … ON TABLE` form emits a `view plm.*` relationGuess key that is dropped *only* because the same file contains the matching `CREATE TABLE` (`check-pr-object-collisions.mjs:584-588`) — splitting these statements across migrations would silently widen the claim surface.\n## Assessment\nNothing here endangers the existing database: the migration is purely additive, creates two empty tables, alters no existing object, and closes access by default. The version reservation, object keys, and access model all hold up under the repo's own guards, and the sealed evidence is accurate where I could check it.\nWhat blocks approval is that the file is presented as the **final** plm home while being structurally weaker than the `dflow` landing table it is meant to replace: it drops both uniqueness invariants, drops every index serving the primary access path, keeps a unique constraint that enforces nothing and cannot be used for lookup, and omits a self-FK plus three intra-`plm` FKs whose targets `#2202` already moved into `plm`. Two of those omissions are defended in the header by a rationale that the repository's own applied migrations and its own `dispatchObjectKeys` policy contradict, and the \"shape matches the dflow source\" claim is untrue for two column defaults and for column order. Since the contract defers row movement, none of this is caught by any test — and no test was added.\nRecommended minimum before re-review: add the self-FK `(source_action_id, rfq_item_id) → (id, rfq_item_id)` and the `plm.\"RFQItem\"`/`plm.\"RFQStep\"` FKs (zero new object keys); restore `item_user_assignment_one_active` and `item_workflow_action_one_return_per_source` plus the `rfq_item_id`-leading lookup indexes (expanding the claim to name the `index plm.*` objects); either match dflow's derived `actor_identity_source`/`actor_identity_email` defaults or drop the \"shape matches\" claim and document the divergence; align column order with the source; add a catalogue-only `to_regclass`/shape assertion; correct or qualify the append-only comment; add a `supabase/tests/` contract test; and update segregation-doc rows 24a/24b. Per AGENTS.md §4, migrations and RLS work require two independent reviewers — this is one.\n> VOIDED REVIEWER LINE - VERDICT: REVISE 87ff50ea3fbb8a76f33f7e7f684e639bfdcaa9e7\n\n> VERDICT LINE VOIDED BY THE GOVERNED REVIEW RUNNER.\n>\n> 2 line(s) that a verdict parser would have read as a decision (REVISE) at this head were rewritten so that no tool can read them as a verdict. Indexes built now, on empty tables, are free; built after the deferred row movement they require a build over a populated table, and `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` cannot run in a transaction — pushing the mover toward a locking build.\n**3. The two deferred UNIQUE indexes are integrity invariants, and deferring them can make them permanently unaddable.** `item_user_assignment_one_active` is the only thing enforcing \"one active assignment per (item, function, user)\" — the plm table keeps the weaker window CHECK (`:26-27`) but permits two rows with `effective_to IS NULL` for the same key. `item_workflow_action_one_return_per_source` is what makes *\"at most one action may close any given source handoff\"* structural rather than conventional (`20260905053422:91-95`). If either table takes writes before these are added, accumulated duplicates make the later `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX` fail, converting a free deferral into a data-cleanup project. Both are free right now.\n**4. The self-referencing composite FK was dropped, while the UNIQUE constraint that exists only to serve it was kept.** `20260905053422:60-65` adds `item_workflow_action_source_action_id_fkey FOREIGN KEY (source_action_id, rfq_item_id) REFERENCES dflow.item_workflow_action(id, rfq_item_id)`. That is a **self-reference**: in the plm home it becomes `plm.item_workflow_action → plm.item_workflow_action`, entirely intra-schema and intra-table. The header's rationale (`:6-8`, cross-schema FKs into `dflow.*`) does not describe it, and no object outside the two claimed tables is touched by adding it. Without it, `source_action_id` may name a nonexistent action **or an action on a different RFQ item** — exactly the hole #2203 exists to close (*\"carrying rfq_item_id through the reference makes it structural, so no future writer … can bind a return to another item's handoff\"*, `:51-55`). The file keeps the cosmetic half (`item_workflow_action_source_action_not_self`, `:58-59`) and drops the half that binds to the same item.\n**This is also the index that exists but cannot be used as written** (mandatory check #1, explicitly): `UNIQUE (id, rfq_item_id)` at `:52` exists in the source *solely* as that FK's target. With the FK absent it is dead weight — an extra btree on a 16-column append-only table whose leading column `id` is already unique via the PK, so it serves no query the PK does not serve better. Either carry the self-FK (which then justifies the constraint) or drop the constraint.\n**5. The FK rationale is factually wrong about which schema the sources point at.** `20260904143518:11-30` (#2202) repointed these FKs **from `dflow` into `plm`**: `item_user_assignment.rfq_item_id → plm.\"RFQItem\"(\"rfqItem_id\") ON DELETE CASCADE NOT VALID`, and `item_workflow_action.rfq_item_id → plm.\"RFQItem\"`, `prior_step_id`/`new_step_id → plm.\"RFQStep\"(\"RFQStep_id\") NOT VALID`. So for four of the six FKs the live sources already target the *same schema* as the new tables. Only the user references are genuinely `dflow`-targeted (`user_id`, `assigned_by_user_id`, `actor_user_id`, `fallback_recipient_user_id → dflow.users(id)`; #2202 did not repoint them). The honest reason to defer the item/step FKs is that an FK installs a trigger on the parent `plm.\"RFQItem\"`/`plm.\"RFQStep\"`, which sits outside the two claimed objects — not that they point at `dflow`.\n**6. \"Column shapes match the dflow sources\" (`:6`) is false for `item_workflow_action` in three specific ways.**\n- **(a) Column order diverges.** Live dflow order appends `actor_identity_source`, `actor_identity_email` **last** (`20260905053422:44-48`; `20260907121732:12-26` — `ADD COLUMN` lands at the end). The plm file inserts them at positions 5-6 (`:40-41`), before `prior_step_id`. Same 16 columns, different ordinal positions. This bites the *deferred row movement* this file explicitly creates: `INSERT INTO plm.item_workflow_action SELECT * FROM dflow.item_workflow_action`, or any `%ROWTYPE`/positional mover, maps by position and would place dflow's `prior_step_id integer` into plm's `actor_identity_source text`. (`plm.item_user_assignment` does match position-for-position, `:15-23` vs `20260901221310:4-13`; the divergence is only in the action table.)\n- **(b) DEFAULT expressions dropped.** Live `actor_identity_source` defaults to a CASE over `pg_catalog.current_setting('request.designflow.actor_id', true)`, and `actor_identity_email` to an expression over that setting plus `auth.jwt() ->> 'email'` (`20260907121732:14-26`). The plm file hardcodes `DEFAULT 'supabase_auth'` (`:40`) and gives `actor_identity_email` **no default** (`:41`). Combined with the carried-over `actor_provenance` CHECK (`:68-74`), an INSERT omitting `actor_identity_source` is forced to `supabase_auth` and must then supply a non-null `actor_auth_user_id` — so the trusted-backend provenance path (#2496's entire purpose) cannot be recorded implicitly in the plm home, and a mover relying on source defaults will misclassify backend-JWT rows or fail the CHECK. Undisclosed in the header.\n- **(c) All column comments dropped.** Sources carry `COMMENT ON COLUMN` for `actor_auth_user_id`, `actor_identity_source`, `actor_identity_email` (`20260907121732:128-134`), `source_action_id`, `fallback_recipient_user_id`, `requires_admin_review` (`20260905053422:510-517`), plus `COMMENT ON CONSTRAINT item_user_assignment_rfq_item_id_fkey` (`20260904143518:272`). The plm file has two table comments only (`:32-33`, `:77-78`). The lost semantics are the non-obvious ones — *\"the ORIGINAL actor is never rewritten; read it through source_action_id\"* and the two-value `actor_identity_source` vocabulary — precisely what a \"final home\" must preserve. The sibling shows the fallback pattern of folding that into the table comment (`20260917022233:64-65`); this file does neither.\n**7. Append-only is asserted in a comment and enforced by nothing.** `:78` comments the table *\"Append-only workflow action history\"*; `:33` describes the other as *\"assignment history\"*. The sources enforce it with triggers `item_user_assignment_immutable_history` → `dflow.reject_item_assignment_history_rewrite()` and `item_workflow_action_immutable` → `dflow.reject_item_workflow_action_rewrite()` (`20260901221310:83-119`). The plm homes have **no triggers and no guard functions**, so UPDATE and DELETE are unrestricted. #2203's design depends on that guarantee (*\"rows remain append-only … which is why the 'handoff is closed' fact is modelled as a child row pointing back at its parent rather than as a flag updated on the parent\"*, `:33-37`). A comment asserting a property the schema does not enforce is a false claim in the catalog.\n### Mandatory check #2 — function volatility: **no defect; here is exactly what I checked**\nThe migration creates **zero** functions, procedures and triggers, so there is no volatility marker in this change that could be wrong. To keep that answer from being vacuous:\n- The three `DEFAULT clock_timestamp()` expressions (`:20`, `:23`, `:47`) do embed a **VOLATILE** function in a column default. (The sibling uses `DEFAULT now()` at `20260917022233:43`; the difference here is deliberate and source-driven.)\n- The two dropped DEFAULT expressions (finding 6b) are the shape's only session-state readers, calling `pg_catalog.current_setting(text, true)` and `auth.jwt()` — both correctly non-IMMUTABLE in the source. Dropping them removes volatility rather than mislabeling it; the cost is behavioral, per 6b.\n- Nothing anywhere in the change is marked `IMMUTABLE`, so the specific bug class named in the brief (a table-reading body marked IMMUTABLE) does not occur. Nothing in the file would have caught that, and nothing will catch a future dflow shape change silently diverging the home.\n- **No post-create catalogue verification** — no `to_regclass` on either new table, no assertion of column count, index inventory, `relrowsecurity = true`, or that the revokes took effect. Any assertions added here must stay catalogue-only: that guard refuses `from plm.<table>` inside a verification block, so use `to_regclass`, `pg_attribute`, `pg_indexes`, `pg_class.relrowsecurity`, `has_table_privilege` — never a data read.\n### MINOR\n**8. Unqualified function calls inside stored CHECK constraints** (`:25`, `:29`, `:55`, `:57`, `:65`): `lower(btrim(…))`, `jsonb_typeof(…)`. Constraint expressions are re-evaluated in the *inserting session's* `search_path`, and `pg_catalog` is implicitly first only when not named in it — so a role with `search_path = public, pg_catalog` and a hostile `public.lower(text)`/`public.jsonb_typeof(jsonb)` could shadow them. The repo's own #2496 defends against exactly this by qualifying: `pg_catalog.lower(nullif(pg_catalog.btrim(…)))` (`20260907121732:19-25`). Inherited from the sources (`20260901221310:6`), but a brand-new table is the cheap place to fix it.\n**9. The access-model rationale comment is missing.** `:80-83` does something that looks alarming without explanation: ENABLE RLS with **zero policies** plus `REVOKE ALL` from `PUBLIC, anon, authenticated, service_role`. The posture is **correct and conventional** — the sibling does the identical thing and says why: *\"Same access model as sibling plm tracking tables: the DesignFlow API connects as the table owner. No browser or service-role access\"* (`20260917022233:66-68`). Zero-policy RLS is a managed state here (see `20260914155226_revoke_api_role_grants_zero_policy_tables.sql`), and it is deliberately the *opposite* of dflow's, whose comment warns that *\"Enabling RLS with no policy would additionally revoke the intended `authenticated` SELECT\"* (`20260901221310:328-336`) because dflow grants SELECT back. Here nothing is granted back, so it is coherent. Only the missing rationale is a gap — and note this is the one place the file *should* have copied the sibling's comment.\n**10. No recorded grant path for the actual production writer.** #2496 establishes that in production the DesignFlow backend connects as the dedicated role `designflow`, not `postgres` (`20260907121732:38-44`, `:116-124`). Revoking from the four roles and granting nothing is right for empty tables, but nothing records that the deferred row-movement session must grant INSERT (and likely SELECT) on both plm tables to that writer role. The sibling's \"connects as the table owner\" assumption should be checked against that role split rather than inherited.\n**11. No `set lock_timeout` / `statement_timeout`** (both sources carry them: `20260905053422:40-41`, `20260907121732:7-8`). Finding 1 is established by reading the guard sources and tracing the exact call path — it is a static-text rule with a fully determined outcome, corroborated by `test_migration_derivation.py:102` — but it was not executed.\n## Assessment\nNothing here endangers an existing application: the change is strictly additive, touches no live object, and its deny-all access posture matches house convention. But it is not mergeable as written. Finding 1 is a hard machine-enforced failure that reddens `main`'s drift guard on merge and makes the version unpromotable to production, and the repo's byte-binding doctrine means it cannot be cleanly repaired afterward. Findings 2-7 show the file's two central claims are untrue — the shapes do **not** match the sources (column order, two defaults, six column comments), and the deferral rationale covers 2 of 6 dropped indexes while misdescribing where 4 of 6 FKs point. It drops two uniqueness invariants, one intra-table self-FK and all append-only enforcement, while its own catalog comment asserts append-only. Final determination at the bottom of this reply.\n## Evidence packet verification\nI verified the seal before judging any code, using read-only tools only (this review profile has no shell, so I could not recompute the digest myself).\n| Check | Result |\n|---|---|\n| `.git/HEAD` in the snapshot | `87ff50ea3fbb8a76f33f7e7f684e639bfdcaa9e7` — matches the injected authoritative head |\n| `identity.json` `head` | `87ff50ea…` — matches |\n| `identity.json` `base` / `merge_base` / `requested_base` | all `a5c1f0fb…` — matches `MANIFEST.md` §2 |\n| `identity.json` `source_digest` | `4d40625ab3d3325b…02fa` — byte-identical to the `MANIFEST.md` whole-source digest |\n| Conversation-start git snapshot | `87ff50ea` → `c5a57705` → `a5c1f0fb`, working tree clean — matches §3 (\"no uncommitted edits\", \"no untracked files\") |\n| `patch.diff` vs. on-disk file | The 85-line migration in `patch.diff` is byte-identical to `supabase/migrations/20260925044029_plm_item_user_assignment_and_workflow_action.sql` (hunk header `@@ -0,0 +1,85 @@` agrees with the file length) |\n| Files changed vs. `contract.json` `allowed_paths` | Exactly the three permitted paths. **No path escape, no out-of-lane write.** |\n| Recompute of `source_digest` | **Not possible** — no shell in this profile. Reported as an evidence gap, not as a pass. |\nThe directory does match the stated base and head, so I reviewed the right change.\n## Coverage statement\nRequired by `docs/agents/anti-collision-summary.md` (a verdict with no coverage statement is not review evidence).\nExamined in full: the migration under review (all 85 lines); both `.agent/work/3498/1/*.json` evidence files; `patch.diff`; `MANIFEST.md`; `identity.json`.\nExamined as governing context: `AGENTS.md`; `docs/agents/anti-collision-summary.md`; `docs/agents/references-and-runbooks.md` §8.1 (exposed schemas); `docs/migration-verification-cost-guard.md`; `scripts/check-sql.sh` (all 542 lines, including Guard B, Guard B2, the #1684 EOL guard, and its two Node sub-guards); `scripts/check-expected-count-patterns.mjs`; `scripts/check-migration-verify-cost.mjs`; `docs/production-promotion-app-tolerance-contract.md` (default-privileges root cause).\nExamined as the authoritative source shape being copied: `supabase/migrations/20260901221310_designflow_item_assignment_action_history.sql`, `20260904143518_canonical_designflow_workflow_contract.sql`, `20260905053422_workflow_action_handoff_integrity.sql`, `20260907121732_designflow_trusted_backend_actor.sql`; plus the live-catalogue snapshot `docs/verification/database-efficiency/20260904T212459Z/run2/{indexes,foreign-keys,functions-security,relation-stats}.csv|json` and `…/20260910T002917Z/api-access-matrix.md`.\nExamined as house-style exemplars: `20260920202755_hts_rag_classification_jobs.sql` (full `$verify$` block), `20260827224547_contract_property_evidence_landing.sql` (`plm` grants/RLS pattern), `20260710135975_reconcile_service_role_grants.sql` (default privileges), and all 13 `grant … on table plm.*` sites in `supabase/migrations/`.\nExamined as contract tests: `supabase/tests/designflow_trusted_backend_actor_contracts.sql`, `designflow_workflow_action_handoff_integrity_contracts.sql`.\n**No tests were run** (manifest §5). I treat that as unknown, not as a pass. `plm` schema DDL cannot be executed from this profile.\n---\n# Findings\n## Blocker\n### B1 — `actor_identity_source` / `actor_identity_email` defaults were replaced, so the plm home cannot record a DesignFlow-JWT actor\n`supabase/migrations/20260925044029_…sql:40-41`\n```sql\nactor_identity_source text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'supabase_auth',\nactor_identity_email text,\n```\nThe live `dflow` source (`20260907121732_designflow_trusted_backend_actor.sql:14-27`) defines these as **dynamic default expressions**, not constants:\n```sql\nadd column actor_identity_source text not null default\n    (case when nullif(pg_catalog.current_setting('request.designflow.actor_id', true), '') is not null\n          then 'designflow_jwt' else 'supabase_auth' end),\nadd column actor_identity_email text default\n    (pg_catalog.lower(nullif(pg_catalog.btrim(coalesce(\n       nullif(pg_catalog.current_setting('request.designflow.actor_email', true), ''),\n       auth.jwt() ->> 'email')), '')));\n```\nThese defaults *are* the provenance mechanism. `dflow.record_item_workflow_action` never supplies either column (`20260905053422:432-438` — the INSERT list omits both), and the contract test asserts the values arrive purely from the defaults:\n`supabase/tests/designflow_trusted_backend_actor_contracts.sql:60-67`\n```sql\nand actor_auth_user_id is null\nand actor_identity_source = 'designflow_jwt'\nand actor_identity_email = '[redacted personal email]'\n) then raise exception 'backend workflow action did not retain truthful DesignFlow-JWT provenance';\n```\nConsequences on the plm home, which copies the `item_workflow_action_actor_provenance` CHECK verbatim at `:68-74`:\n1. A trusted backend write (which sets `request.designflow.actor_id` and leaves `actor_auth_user_id` NULL) now defaults `actor_identity_source` to `'supabase_auth'`. That row has `actor_identity_source = 'supabase_auth' AND actor_auth_user_id IS NULL`, which fails both branches of the copied CHECK → **`23514 check_violation`, the write is rejected.**\n2. If a writer works around it by supplying `actor_auth_user_id`, the action is **recorded as Supabase-auth-attributed when it was not** — silent mis-attribution on an append-only actor-attribution audit table. That is precisely the defect issue #2496 was written to close.\n3. `actor_identity_email` has **no default at all** in plm, so the `designflow_jwt` branch (which requires `actor_identity_email IS NOT NULL`) can never be satisfied by a default-driven write.\nThe migration header asserts at `:6` \"**Column shapes match the dflow sources**\" and the table comment at `:78` repeats \"Shape matches the dflow source\". A column default is part of a column's shape (`pg_attrdef` / `pg_get_expr(adbin, adrelid)`). The claim is false, and the divergence is load-bearing rather than cosmetic.\n*Fix:* copy both default expressions verbatim, or drop the `actor_provenance` CHECK until they are copied. Either way the header claim must be corrected.\n---\n### B2 — The one index this migration adds cannot be used as written\n`:52`\n```sql\nCONSTRAINT item_workflow_action_id_rfq_item_key UNIQUE (id, rfq_item_id),\n```\n`id` is the primary key (`:37`). Any unique constraint whose **leading** column is already unique is trivially satisfied and its backing b-tree is redundant with `item_workflow_action_pkey` for every access path: a lookup on `id` uses the PK; a lookup on `rfq_item_id` cannot use this index at all, because `rfq_item_id` is the *second* key column. So this index serves no query the PK does not already serve, while costing a second b-tree maintenance on every INSERT to an append-only history table.\nThere is exactly one legitimate reason for this constraint to exist, and the migration states it nowhere. In the source it is the **referent of a composite self-FK**:\n`20260905053422_workflow_action_handoff_integrity.sql:57-70`\n```sql\n-- The self-reference is COMPOSITE on purpose: a return may only answer a\n-- handoff recorded against the SAME RFQ item.\nalter table dflow.item_workflow_action\n  add constraint item_workflow_action_id_rfq_item_key unique (id, rfq_item_id);\nalter table dflow.item_workflow_action\n  add constraint item_workflow_action_source_action_id_fkey\n    foreign key (source_action_id, rfq_item_id)\n    references dflow.item_workflow_action(id, rfq_item_id) on delete restrict;\n```\nThe PR copies the UNIQUE **half** of that pair and omits the FK it exists to support. `source_action_id` is present (`:48`) and unconstrained beyond `source_action_id <> id` (`:58-59`), so on the plm home a return **can** be bound to a handoff on a different RFQ item — the exact corruption the composite reference was made structural to prevent. This is an orphaned index plus a lost integrity rule.\nNote also that this FK is **intra-table** (self-referencing `plm.item_workflow_action`), so it writes only a claimed table. The header's deferral rationale at `:7-8` does not cover it.\n*Fix:* either copy `item_workflow_action_source_action_id_fkey` (in-scope, self-referential), or drop `item_workflow_action_id_rfq_item_key` and say why.\n---\n### B3 — Both integrity-enforcing partial unique indexes are missing, and the stated reason for deferring them is self-refuting\nHeader `:9-10`:\n```\n-- Partial unique indexes from the dflow sources are also deferred: this claim\n-- writes exactly the two tables.\n```\nThat justification does not hold. An index **on `plm.item_user_assignment`** or **on `plm.item_workflow_action`** writes only that one table — both are inside the claim's own boundary (`contract.json` `db_writes`). Deferring them was a choice, not a constraint, and the reason given is not the real reason.\nWhat is lost:\n| Missing | Source | Invariant no longer enforced on the plm home |\n|---|---|---|\n| `item_user_assignment_one_active` UNIQUE `(rfq_item_id, function_key, user_id) WHERE effective_to IS NULL` | `20260901221310:18-20` | At most **one active** assignment per item/function/user. Without it the plm home accepts two simultaneously-active holders of the same role on the same item. |\n| `item_workflow_action_one_return_per_source` UNIQUE `(source_action_id) WHERE source_action_id IS NOT NULL` | `20260905053422:100-102` | At most **one return** may close a given handoff. `20260905053422:12-16` states this is the whole point of that migration: *\"so one handoff can never be returned twice.\"* |\nThe first is the invariant the notification fan-out depends on (`20260905053422:411-416` selects active assignees and would double-notify); the second is the invariant that makes \"is this handoff still open?\" a well-formed question. A \"final home\" that silently drops both is not a faithful destination for the rows that will be moved into it — a copy that violates them would land without error.\n---\n### B4 — No index leads with `rfq_item_id` on either table, so every item-scoped access path is a sequential scan\nNeither `CREATE TABLE` is followed by a single `CREATE INDEX`. The only indexes are the two PKs and the two UNIQUE constraints at `:52-53`. Four access-path indexes from the sources are absent:\n| Missing index | Source | Query it serves |\n|---|---|---|\n| `item_user_assignment_active_lookup` `(rfq_item_id, function_key, effective_from, id) INCLUDE (user_id) WHERE effective_to IS NULL` | `20260901221310:22-25` | `set_item_user_assignment`'s `FOR UPDATE` lookup and the notification fan-out `where a.rfq_item_id = … and a.function_key = v_to and a.effective_to is null` (`20260905053422:411-416`) |\n| `item_workflow_action_item_time` `(rfq_item_id, occurred_at, id)` | `20260901221310:41-42` | Per-item action history in time order |\n| `item_workflow_action_open_handoff_lookup` `(rfq_item_id, occurred_at desc, id desc) INCLUDE (actor_user_id)` | `20260905053422:105-107` | *\"the latest still-open handoff on this item in this direction\"* — the `order by a.occurred_at desc, a.id desc limit 1` at `20260905053422:395-408` |\n| `item_workflow_action_admin_review` `(rfq_item_id, occurred_at) WHERE requires_admin_review` | `20260905053422:109-111` | Admin-review queue; `requires_admin_review` is copied at `:51` with no index to serve it |\n`rfq_item_id` is the partition key of an item-master table (it is how the segregation map files both tables — `docs/designflow-master-data-migration/designflow-schema-segregation.md:152-153`). On the plm home there is **no index whose leading column is `rfq_item_id`** on either table. Every item-scoped read, and every `NOT EXISTS (select 1 … where r.source_action_id = h.id)` open-handoff probe, degrades to a full scan. These tables were 32 768 rows / 8 192 pages at the 2026-09-04 snapshot and are append-only, so they only grow.\n`scripts/check-migration-verify-cost.mjs` and `docs/migration-verification-cost-guard.md` explain why *verification* must not scan `plm.*` inside the apply transaction — that is an argument for catalogue-only checks, not an argument against creating the indexes the runtime needs.\n---\n### B5 — `REVOKE ALL … FROM service_role` with no compensating GRANT strips a live repo-wide standing privilege\n`:82-83`\n```sql\nREVOKE ALL ON TABLE plm.item_user_assignment FROM PUBLIC, anon, authenticated, service_role;\nREVOKE ALL ON TABLE plm.item_workflow_action FROM PUBLIC, anon, authenticated, service_role;\n```\nThis is not a no-op. `20260710135975_reconcile_service_role_grants.sql:14` is applied and in force:\n```sql\nalter default privileges in schema plm grant all on tables to service_role;\n```\n`docs/production-promotion-app-tolerance-contract.md:475-477` records this explicitly as live: *\"`20260710135975` set a schema-wide `alter default privileges … to service_role`, which fires at `CREATE TABLE`.\"* So `service_role` acquires ALL on both tables at creation, and these two REVOKEs **actively remove it**.\nEvery other `plm` table in the repo does the opposite. All 13 `grant … on table plm.*` sites grant to `service_role`, and the closest structural sibling pairs the revoke with a grant in the same file:\n`20260827224547_contract_property_evidence_landing.sql:88-95`\n```sql\nrevoke all on table plm.contract_property_capture from public, anon, authenticated, service_role;\n…\ngrant select, insert on table plm.contract_property_capture to service_role;\n```\n`20260920202755_hts_rag_classification_jobs.sql:73-77` follows the same revoke-then-grant shape. **No `plm` table in this repository has ever been left with a bare REVOKE and no GRANT.**\nImpact: `plm` is not in `pgrst.db_schemas` (`docs/agents/references-and-runbooks.md:21` — `public, graphql_public, api, crm, pim, core, app`), so `anon`/`authenticated` could not reach these tables over PostgREST anyway; those two revokes are harmless belt-and-braces. The `service_role` revoke is the one that bites. The stated purpose of these tables is to be the home the DesignFlow migration session moves rows into and that DesignFlow's backend then writes. As landed, any non-owner role gets `permission denied for table item_user_assignment`. Only `postgres` (the migration/owner role) can write. The hand-off named in the migration's own header (`:5-6`) is blocked by the migration itself.\n`docs/agents/anti-collision-summary.md:172` states the rule this violates: *\"an RLS policy is **not** a GRANT — a browser-writable app table needs both.\"* Here there is neither.\n---\n### B6 — No exact-object self-verification block anywhere in the migration\nThis is mandated review check #3, and the change asserts **nothing**. There is no `DO $verify$ … $verify$`, no `to_regclass`, no `pg_attribute` / `pg_constraint` / `pg_indexes` / `pg_policies` / `has_table_privilege` probe, no `raise exception` on mismatch. The file ends at `COMMIT;` (`:85`).\nWhat it depends on and merely *infers*:\n- that the `plm` schema exists — never checked (`CREATE TABLE plm.x` fails with `3F000` if not, which is at least loud, but the error is not the assertion the house style makes);\n- that neither table already exists — `CREATE TABLE` without `IF NOT EXISTS` and without a pre-check;\n- that `plm.\"RFQItem\"` / `plm.\"RFQStep\"` exist, which the FK rationale at `:7-8` implicitly rests on — never checked;\n- that the copied CHECK predicates and the copied UNIQUE constraint actually landed with the intended definitions — never checked;\n- that RLS is on and privileges are as intended — never checked.\nThe repository mandates the opposite. `docs/agents/anti-collision-summary.md:156-157` (§4 rule 5, verbatim in `docs/agents/section-4-anti-collision-rules.md:1176`):\n> **Before trusting any migration, confirm the OBJECT exists (`to_regclass`) — never just the ledger row.**\nAnd such a block is *permitted* here — the verify-cost guard exists to steer verification toward catalogue-only checks, not to forbid them. `docs/migration-verification-cost-guard.md:38-44`:\n> Naming a prohibited object inside a catalogue lookup or an error message is **allowed**, because nothing scans it: `to_regclass(…)`, `pg_get_viewdef('…'::regclass)`, `has_table_privilege(…)`, `information_schema.columns where table_schema = 'plm'` … all pass. That catalogue-only shape is what the guard exists to steer verification towards.\nThe house exemplar is `20260920202755_hts_rag_classification_jobs.sql:106-183`, whose `$verify$` block asserts, with exact-object precision: relation kind + `relrowsecurity` via `pg_class`/`pg_namespace`; the FK by `confrelid`, `confdeltype` **and** the exact `pg_get_constraintdef(oid)` string; the UNIQUE by exact definition string; the exact policy count from `pg_policies`; a column by `atttypid` + `attnotnull` + absence of any `pg_attrdef` row; each policy by name, `cmd`, `roles`, `qual` and `with_check`; grants by `has_table_privilege` / `has_column_privilege` with an exact `string_agg` column list; and role attributes from `pg_roles`. Its own comment at `:105` says why: *\"Fail the apply on a wrong catalog contract, in addition to behavioral CI.\"*\nA had-this-block check would have caught B1 (the `pg_attrdef` mismatch), B2 (the orphaned unique with no matching FK), B3/B4 (missing indexes) and B5 (the missing `service_role` grant) at apply time instead of at review time.\n---\n### B7 — The FK deferral rationale is factually wrong: the referents already live in `plm`\nHeader `:6-8`:\n```\n-- Cross-schema foreign keys into dflow.* are deliberately omitted so the plm\n-- homes do not couple to the landing schema; referential integrity is wired\n-- when rows move.\n```\n`rfq_item_id`, `prior_step_id` and `new_step_id` do **not** reference `dflow.*`. `20260904143518_canonical_designflow_workflow_contract.sql` re-pointed all of them at `plm` on 2026-09-04:\n```sql\n:13  foreign key (rfq_item_id)  references plm.\"RFQItem\"(\"rfqItem_id\") on delete cascade  not valid\n:21  foreign key (rfq_item_id)  references plm.\"RFQItem\"(\"rfqItem_id\") on delete restrict not valid\n:24  foreign key (prior_step_id) references plm.\"RFQStep\"(\"RFQStep_id\") not valid\n:27  foreign key (new_step_id)   references plm.\"RFQStep\"(\"RFQStep_id\") not valid\n```\n`20260905053422` and its function bodies confirm the referents are `plm.\"RFQItem\"` / `plm.\"RFQStep\"` (`:359`, `:376`, `:458`), and `plm.\"itemHeader\"` / `plm.\"productUserAssignment\"` exist in the same schema (`supabase/ci-bootstrap/010_pre_adoption_baseline.sql:1634`, `:6406`).\nSo these three FKs would be **intra-`plm`** — no coupling to the landing schema whatsoever, and an FK adds a constraint (and its supporting index) to the *child* table only, i.e. to a table this claim already owns. The stated reason for omitting them is contradicted by the repository. Only `user_id`, `assigned_by_user_id`, `actor_user_id` and `fallback_recipient_user_id` genuinely point at `dflow.users`, and only those are defensible deferrals.\nBecause `plm.\"RFQItem\"` already exists, `plm.item_user_assignment` and `plm.item_workflow_action` can right now hold an `rfq_item_id` that matches no item — dangling by construction, in the schema that is supposed to be the canonical item master.\n---\n## High\n### H1 — `ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` with zero policies, contradicting the source migration's explicit warning and the sibling `plm` pattern\n`:80-81` enable RLS; no `CREATE POLICY` appears anywhere in the file.\nThe repository has already measured what this means. `docs/verification/database-efficiency/20260910T002917Z/api-access-matrix.md:88`, describing four tables in exactly this state:\n> Every read returns count 0 … because **RLS with no policy denies all**.\nAnd the source migration for these very tables reasoned about the identical situation and chose the opposite, `20260901221310:331-337`:\n> so row-level security is deliberately not enabled here: there is no direct-write path for RLS to police … **Enabling RLS with no policy would additionally revoke the intended `authenticated` SELECT.**\nTwo further gaps against the sibling `plm` pattern:\n- `plm` tables that do use RLS pair `enable` with **`force`** — `20260827224547:80-87` issues `alter table plm.contract_property_capture force row level security;` for all four. Without `FORCE`, the table owner and any `BYPASSRLS` role are exempt, so \"RLS is on\" is not a uniform guarantee.\n- `20260920202755:95-104` creates six policies alongside its `enable row level security`, then asserts the exact count in its `$verify$` block (`:129-131`).\nCombined with B5 the tables are triple-locked: no privilege, no policy, RLS on. That may be a deliberate \"closed until wired\" posture — but it is asserted nowhere in the file, it is not the `plm` convention, and it is the exact configuration the source migration warns against. If it is intended, it needs to be stated and verified; if it is not, it needs `FORCE` plus policies plus grants.\n### H2 — Append-only enforcement is omitted while the table comment asserts it\n`:78`\n```\n'… Append-only workflow action history. Shape matches the dflow source; …'\n```\nNothing enforces append-only. The source installs row triggers that reject every UPDATE and DELETE:\n- `20260901221310:127` — `create trigger item_user_assignment_immutable_history before update or delete on dflow.item_user_assignment … execute function dflow.reject_item_assignment_history_rewrite();`\n- `20260901221310:141` — `create trigger item_workflow_action_immutable before update or delete on dflow.item_workflow_action …`\nNeither trigger nor either function is reproduced. The plm home is freely rewritable and deletable, so a comment claiming a property the object does not have is now in the catalogue. `20260905053422:36-40` explains why append-only is structural rather than decorative for this table: it is *why* \"handoff is closed\" is modelled as a child row pointing at its parent instead of a flag on the parent.\nRelated: `docs/production-promotion-app-tolerance-contract.md:456-458` warns that `TRUNCATE` does not fire row triggers and `service_role` holds TRUNCATE via the default privileges. Once B5 is fixed by restoring `service_role` ALL, that exposure applies here too unless the grant is column/verb-scoped as `20260920202755:78-85` does.\n### H3 — `item_workflow_action_return_names_its_source` CHECK was not copied, although both columns it governs were\n`20260905053422:186-193`\n```sql\nadd constraint item_workflow_action_return_names_its_source\n  check (routing_context ->> 'return_to_original_handoff' is distinct from 'true'\n         or source_action_id is not null);\n```\n`:46` copies `routing_context` and `:48` copies `source_action_id`, and `:54-67` copies three other CHECKs from the same source migration (`action_key_shape`, `routing_context_object`, `source_action_not_self`, `fallback_is_labeled`). This one is skipped. The constraint set is therefore a cherry-picked subset, which is a second, independent falsification of \"shape matches the dflow source\". On the plm home a return action may leave `source_action_id` NULL — the \"unclosable open handoff\" state that `20260905053422:180-185` says must \"stop the apply loudly\".\n### H4 — `GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY` blocks the row movement the migration exists to prepare for, and the sequence gap is unaddressed\n`:15` and `:37` both use `GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY`. A migration that copies `dflow.item_user_assignment` rows into `plm.item_user_assignment` preserving `id` must use `OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE`, and must then advance the identity sequence past `max(id)` or the first native insert collides. The dflow sources use the identical construct (`20260901221310:4`, `:27`), so parity is preserved — but neither the header (`:5-6`, \"row movement belongs to the DesignFlow migration session\"), the table comments, nor `completion.json` `assumptions_resolved` records this obligation for the session that inherits it. `20260905053422` handled the analogous inherited-state problem explicitly and at length (`:112-176`); this migration is silent.\n---\n## Medium\n### M1 — `-- derived-from:` breaks the repository's machine-readable lineage convention\n`:3`\n```\n-- derived-from: dflow.item_user_assignment, dflow.item_workflow_action (live shapes)\n```\nAcross 119 migrations the value is **`none` or one or more 14-digit migration versions** — e.g. `20260905053422:3` `-- derived-from: 20260904143518`; `20260907121732:5` `-- derived-from: 20260901221310`; `20260829004145:4` `-- derived-from: 20260823175638, 20260825192610`; `20260827224547:1` `-- derived-from: none`. Object names appear nowhere else. The correct value here is `20260901221310, 20260904143518, 20260905053422, 20260907121732`.\nThe parenthetical \"(live shapes)\" is additionally unverifiable from this packet — manifest §5 records no tests and no DB read artifact, and `contract.json` `db_reads` claims reads of the two `dflow` tables that the SQL itself never performs (it contains no `SELECT`). Given B1 and H3, the produced shape demonstrably does *not* match the live shape, so the claim is contradicted by the file it heads.\n### M2 — `lock_timeout` / `statement_timeout` not set, unlike every comparable DDL migration\n`20260905053422:38-39` and `20260907121732:8-9` both open with:\n```sql\nset lock_timeout = '5s';\nset statement_timeout = '5min';\n```\nThe PR goes straight from the header to `BEGIN;` (`:12`). For two empty `CREATE TABLE`s the blast radius is small, but `CREATE TABLE` still takes an `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock on the new relation and touches `pg_type`/`pg_class`, and the surrounding `plm` namespace is shared with live DesignFlow traffic. The house pattern costs two lines.\n### M3 — Evidence gaps in `completion.json`\n`.agent/work/3498/1/completion.json:23-38` records three checks. Two problems:\n1. **Guard B2 never ran.** `check-sql.sh:404-433` only executes the live-ledger comparison when `CHECK_SQL_PREVIEW_LEDGER` / `CHECK_SQL_PRODUCTION_LEDGER` or the corresponding `_DB_URL` variables are set; otherwise it emits a WARNING and skips (`:421-433`). The recorded evidence string lists \"Guard B, expected-count, verify-cost, EOL reference\" — Guard B2 is conspicuously absent. Guard B (`:246-273`) only compares against the *base branch*, which `check-sql.sh:283-296` documents as a real blind spot: *\"a branch can add a version that sorts after main's newest and STILL be behind what preview has already applied.\"* That blind spot is the entire subject of §4 rule 5, which has already caused two silent skips. Locally I can confirm `20260925044029` is the only `20260925*` file and is the newest version in `supabase/migrations/`, so Guard B passes trivially — but no evidence in this packet establishes it against either live ledger.\n2. **The version reservation is not verifiable from this snapshot.** §4 rule 1 makes the dispatch-created GitHub issue body authoritative for the lane, the exact-object claim and the reserved version; `contract.json:29` asserts *\"claim #3502 reserves 20260925044029\"*. Nothing in the repository contains the string `20260925044029` outside the migration filename and the two `.agent` files, and the lane ledger is GitHub-backed rather than a repo file. I could not confirm the reservation or that `plm.item_user_assignment` / `plm.item_workflow_action` are not claimed by another open lane. This is an access limit of the packet, not a defect I can prove — but the orchestrator should confirm it before merge, since \"Cross-PR object collision\" is only a backstop (`anti-collision-summary.md:104-106`).\nAlso note `anti-collision-summary.md:61-62`: *\"Scripts/docs/CI-only work needs one independent reviewer. **Migrations, data movement, production applies, and security/RLS work still need two.**\"* This change is a migration **and** RLS work, so it requires two independent exact-head reviews.\n### M4 — The segregation map now contradicts the schema\n`docs/designflow-master-data-migration/designflow-schema-segregation.md:152-153` still reads, for both rows: *\"`plm` table not yet created\"*. After this migration that is false. The changelog at `:328` records the 2026-09-24 placement decision but not the creation.\nI am **not** faulting the author: `contract.json:12-16` `allowed_paths` permits only the migration and the two `.agent` files, and `prohibited_actions` forbids writing outside them, so updating the doc was correctly out of lane. This is a follow-up the orchestrator must schedule, flagged so it is not lost.\n---\n## Low / informational\n- **L1 — No column comments.** The sources comment the load-bearing columns (`20260905053422:497-503` on `source_action_id` and `fallback_recipient_user_id`; `20260907121732:128-133` on all three actor-identity columns, including the one that explains why `actor_auth_user_id` is NULL). Four adjacent facts I did verify:\n1. **`clock_timestamp()` as a column DEFAULT is correct, and correctly VOLATILE.** Used at `:20`, `:23` and `:47`. `clock_timestamp()` is VOLATILE (wall-clock, advances within a transaction); `now()` / `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP` / `transaction_timestamp()` are STABLE (fixed for the whole transaction). For a table that the DesignFlow session will bulk-copy rows into, a STABLE default would stamp **every** migrated row with one identical timestamp and destroy the `effective_from` / `occurred_at` ordering that `item_workflow_action_open_handoff_lookup` and the `order by a.occurred_at desc, a.id desc` handoff resolution depend on. The VOLATILE choice matches the sources exactly (`20260901221310:9,12,38`). **No finding.**\n2. **No marker is looser than its body, because there is no body.** Nothing here reads a table and claims `IMMUTABLE`. Had the migration copied `dflow.current_designflow_user_id()` it would have had to be `STABLE` (it reads `dflow.users` and `auth.jwt()`; the source correctly marks it `stable` at `20260901221310:60` and the live catalogue records it `s`-class) — but it does not copy it.\n3. **The default expression B1 drops is the volatility-relevant one.** `20260907121732:14-27`'s default reads `pg_catalog.current_setting(text, true)` (STABLE) and `auth.jwt()` (STABLE). Replacing that STABLE-bodied expression with the **constant** `'supabase_auth'` turns a volatile-in-practice, session-aware default into a literal — which is the mechanism of B1, and which any future `pg_get_expr(adbin, adrelid)` parity check between `dflow` and `plm` will flag as a mismatch.\n4. **The omitted trigger functions are VOLATILE by default in the source** (`dflow.reject_item_assignment_history_rewrite`, `dflow.reject_item_workflow_action_rewrite`, `20260901221310:93-141`, no explicit marker → VOLATILE, correct for trigger functions that `raise`). Their omission is H2, not a volatility defect.\nFor completeness, the live catalogue records the two `dflow` writers that will eventually target these tables as `volatility: \"v\"`, `security_definer: true`, `proconfig: search_path=pg_catalog, dflow, auth` (`run2/functions-security.json:1208-1218`, `:1236-1246`) — both correct for bodies that write tables and read `auth.uid()`. When they are re-pointed at `plm`, their `proconfig` search_path must gain `plm`; nothing in this PR prepares for that.\n---\n## What is right, and why this is REVISE rather than REJECT\n- **Genuinely additive and non-destructive.** No `DROP`, no `ALTER` of an existing object, no `TRUNCATE`, no row movement. §4 rule 3 (expand, then contract) is satisfied, and §0.0-B is respected — this changes shape, not contents.\n- **Version hygiene is clean locally.** `20260925044029` is unique across `supabase/migrations/`, is the newest version in the tree, and sorts after the base branch's newest, so §4 rules 4 and 5 hold and Guard B passes. The file is new, so `scripts/check-applied-migration-edit.mjs` has nothing to object to.\n- **The two `#1235`/`#1285` guards pass legitimately**, not by evasion: `check-expected-count-patterns.mjs` only inspects migrations referencing `expected_counts` (this one has none), and `check-migration-verify-cost.mjs` only refuses *reads* inside verification blocks (there is no verification block, and no `SET search_path` statement). Note \"EOL reference\" in `completion.json:26` means the **end-of-life combined table** guard, not line endings; there is no `.gitattributes` in this repository, so that reading is the correct one and the evidence string is accurate on that point.\n- **`plm.item_user_assignment`'s column set is a faithful copy.** Name-for-name, type-for-type, nullability-for-nullability against `20260901221310:3-15`, with the two anonymous source CHECKs promoted to named constraints carrying byte-identical predicates (`:24-29` vs. `20260901221310:6,13,14`).
